identifiers.title: The impact of daily caffeine intake on nighttime sleep in young adult men
identifiers.authors: Weibel J, Lin YS, Landolt HP, Kistler J, Rehm S, Rentsch KM, Slawik H, Borgwardt S, Cajochen C, Reichert CF
identifiers.citation: Weibel J, Lin YS, Landolt HP, et al. The impact of daily caffeine intake on nighttime sleep in young adult men. Sci Rep. 2021;11(1):4668.

design.quote: We employed a double-blind, randomized, crossover study including a caffeine, a withdrawal, and a placebo condition.

species.quote: Twenty male volunteers were recruited into the present study through online advertisements and flyers distributed in public areas.

population.value: healthy men aged 18 to 35 who habitually consume 300 to 600 mg of caffeine a day and sleep well
population.quote: Interested individuals aged between 18 and 35 years old (mean age ± SD: 26.4 ± 4 years) and reporting a daily caffeine consumption between 300 and 600 mg (mean intake ± SD: 478.1 ± 102.8 mg) were included.

sampleSize.quote: Twenty male volunteers were recruited into the present study through online advertisements and flyers distributed in public areas.

facts.label: Number and sex of participants
facts.value: Twenty male volunteers
facts.quote: Twenty male volunteers were recruited into the present study through online advertisements and flyers distributed in public areas.

facts.label: Age range and habitual caffeine intake
facts.value: aged between 18 and 35 years old
facts.quote: Interested individuals aged between 18 and 35 years old (mean age ± SD: 26.4 ± 4 years) and reporting a daily caffeine consumption between 300 and 600 mg (mean intake ± SD: 478.1 ± 102.8 mg) were included.

facts.label: Participants were good sleepers
facts.value: good sleep quality
facts.quote: all volunteers reported good sleep quality assessed with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI; score ≤ 5)

facts.label: Trial design
facts.value: double-blind, randomized, crossover study
facts.quote: We employed a double-blind, randomized, crossover study including a caffeine, a withdrawal, and a placebo condition.

facts.label: The three conditions and the dose
facts.value: 3 × 150 mg caffeine daily
facts.quote: caffeine (3 × 150 mg caffeine daily), withdrawal (3 × 150 mg caffeine for 8 days, then switch to placebo), and placebo (3 × placebo daily)

facts.label: When the capsules were taken
facts.value: 45 min, 255 min, and 475 min after awakening
facts.quote: three times daily, scheduled at 45 min, 255 min, and 475 min after awakening, for a duration of 10 days

facts.label: When sleep was recorded relative to the last caffeine dose
facts.value: starting 8 (caffeine condition) and 15 h (withdrawal condition) after the last caffeine intake
facts.quote: After 9 days of continuous treatment, electroencephalographically (EEG)-derived sleep structure and intensity were recorded during a scheduled 8-h nighttime sleep episode starting 8 (caffeine condition) and 15 h (withdrawal condition) after the last caffeine intake.

facts.label: Sleep schedule participants were asked to keep at home
facts.value: ± 30 min of self-selected bedtime
facts.quote: volunteers were asked to maintain a regular sleep-wake rhythm (± 30 min of self-selected bedtime/wake-up time, 8 h in bed, no daytime napping)

facts.label: no significant difference from placebo (p > 0.05); the text reports no effect size
facts.value: did not reveal significant differences in total sleep time
facts.quote: the analyses of the polysomnography (PSG) did not reveal significant differences in total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency (SE), sleep latencies, or the relative amount of sleep stages among the three conditions (> 0.05)
facts.outcome: Total sleep time, time to fall asleep and sleep stages

facts.label: no significant difference between conditions (p > 0.05)
facts.value: did not reveal significant differences among the three conditions
facts.quote: Analyses of subjective sleep quality assessed with the Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire (LSEQ) did not reveal significant differences among the three conditions in any of the four domains of sleep quality (> 0.05)

facts.label: The predicted loss of deep sleep was not found
facts.value: could not confirm our assumption of a caffeine-induced reduction of sleep depth
facts.quote: Taken together, we could not confirm our assumption of a caffeine-induced reduction of sleep depth, neither in terms of shorter SWS nor in terms of reduced SWA in the caffeine compared to the placebo condition.

facts.label: lower than placebo in both the caffeine and withdrawal conditions (p < 0.05)
facts.value: power density was significantly reduced compared to placebo in the sigma range
facts.quote: power density was significantly reduced compared to placebo in the sigma range during both withdrawal
facts.outcome: Sigma-band brain activity during non-REM sleep

facts.label: Authors' interpretation of the sigma change
facts.value: early signs of caffeine withdrawal
facts.quote: These subtle alterations point to early signs of caffeine withdrawal in the homeostatic aspect of sleep-wake regulation which are already present as early as 8 h after the last caffeine intake.

facts.label: Habitual consumers may reverse overnight withdrawal with the first dose each day
facts.value: chronic consumers reverse daily by the first caffeine dose
facts.quote: This reduction might reflect withdrawal symptoms which chronic consumers reverse daily by the first caffeine dose.

facts.label: Bedtime at home was later on caffeine
facts.value: on average around 25 min later
facts.quote: the ambulatory sleep episodes were on average around 25 min later as compared to placebo

facts.label: How caffeine acts, as the authors describe it: it blocks adenosine receptors and may hold back sleep pressure
facts.value: blocks the
facts.quote: Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist, which blocks the Aand Aadenosine receptors in the central nervous system. It may, thus, attenuate the increase in sleep pressure during wakefulness

facts.label: What earlier work reports for caffeine taken in the evening
facts.value: prolongs sleep latency
facts.quote: caffeine consumed in the evening hours prolongs sleep latency, reduces total sleep time (TST), shortens deep sleep

facts.label: The result may not hold after several days without caffeine
facts.value: do not preclude potential impairments of nighttime sleep after morning caffeine intake
facts.quote: Importantly, our findings do not preclude potential impairments of nighttime sleep after morning caffeine intake, if preceded by several days of abstinence from the stimulant.

facts.label: Earlier work on tolerance, cited by the authors
facts.value: a 1-week treatment of caffeine reduced the sleep disrupting effects
facts.quote: Accordingly, a 1-week treatment of caffeine reduced the sleep disrupting effects, even under conditions of high evening dosages.

facts.label: Only young adults
facts.value: cannot be generalized to other age groups
facts.quote: Thus, the present results cannot be generalized to other age groups such as to middle-aged consumers which are more vulnerable to the caffeine-induced effects on sleep.

facts.label: Small sample
facts.value: only a limited number of participants were studied
facts.quote: Second, only a limited number of participants were studied.

facts.value: only male volunteers were included
facts.quote: only male volunteers were included which clearly reduces the generalizability of the findings
